audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, rule 01 001' (final stress on the main syllable of sesquisyllabic/disyllabic and trisyllabic words) rests on Suwilai 1996 MKS 26 p.166. We held no copy; I fetched sources the open sealang PDF, scanned pp.165-167, and found the quotation verbatim at the stated page, with the trisyllabic template also final-stressed. I also fetched sources the second Glottolog phonology (Waiyanont 1998 Mahidol MA, Lao variety, open on sealang's Mahidol archive) and scanned its stress chapter: it independently states strong stress on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words, stress predictable, adding only a weak-stress grade on closed presyllables (no bearing on primary-stress position). The remaining Glottolog item, Srisakorn 2008 PhD grammar, is not openly available (Mahidol IR, no bitstream) and, coming from the same Mahidol program under the same description tradition, is unlikely to change a

sources.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat 1996, MKS 26:161-178, p.166, PDF from sealang.net/archives/mks
sources.quote: Like other Mon-Khmer languages, the stress is always on the main syllable which is the last syllable of the word. The presyllable always gets the reduced stress and transitional vowel.

sources.citation: Nuchanart Waiyanont. 1998. Thavung phonology at Muang Khamkert, Bolikhamxai Province, Lao P.D.R. MA thesis, Mahidol University. 147 pp. (sealang.net/archives/mahidol/)
sources.quote: p.75: 'The strong stress falls on the monosyllabic word and on the last position of disyllabic word and trisyllabic word. The unstress occur before the last syllable of the word.' p.76-77: three levels — strong stress always on the major (final) syllable; weak stress on closed presyllables; open presyllables unstressed; 'Stress in the Samhing Thavung is predictable'. p.79: trisyllabic [CVC.CV.'CV], strong stress on the third syllable.
sources.locator: printed p.75 sec. 4.4; pp.76-79 ch. V sec. 5.2-5.3 (PDF pp.88-92; scanned in w_ocr/)

sources.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat. 1996. Phonological characteristics of So (Thavung), a Vietic language of Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 26: 161-178.
sources.quote: 'Like other Mon-Khmer languages, the stress is always on the main syllable which is the last syllable of the word. The presyllable always gets the reduced stress and transitional vowel.' Word = 1-3 syllables; trisyllabic template CV(C)CV'CV(C) (final stress).
